items.followUp: Differentiate between hypertonic and hypotonic solutions in relation to a cell.

rubric.why: Tests understanding of hypertonic solutions and osmosis.
rubric.description: Defines a hypertonic solution relative to the cell and states the direction of water movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it has a higher solute concentration than the cell and water moves out of the cell by osmosis. Accept an equivalent description of greater concentration outside the cell causing water loss from it.

rubric.why: Tests understanding of hypotonic solutions and osmosis.
rubric.description: Defines a hypotonic solution relative to the cell and states the direction of water movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it has a lower solute concentration than the cell and water moves into the cell by osmosis. Accept an equivalent description of lower concentration outside the cell causing water gain.

modelAnswer: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis.
A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water moves into the cell by osmosis.

items.followUp: Name four animals that are endangered or threatened with extinction.

rubric.why: Checks that an extinct animal is correctly named.
rubric.how: Award ½ mark for each correct extinct animal, up to 1 mark for two. Accept any valid examples, including dinosaurs, dodo, mammoth, passenger pigeon or Tasmanian tiger.

rubric.why: Checks that further examples are correctly named.
rubric.how: Award ½ mark for each additional correct extinct animal, up to 1 mark for two. Accept any valid examples; do not award twice for the same animal.

items.followUp: State two differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: Tests a defining feature of organisms in kingdom Monera.
rubric.description: States that Monera are prokaryotic and lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Monera as prokaryotic or stating that its cells lack a true nucleus/nuclear membrane.

rubric.why: Tests the contrasting cell type of organisms in kingdom Protista.
rubric.description: States that Protista are eukaryotic and have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Protista as eukaryotic or stating that its cells have a true nucleus/nuclear membrane.

modelAnswer: Monera are prokaryotic organisms; their cells lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
Protista are eukaryotic organisms; their cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.

items.followUp: Why is eucalyptus sometimes planted in waterlogged areas?

rubric.why: Tests recognition of the plant's growth characteristic.
rubric.description: Identifies eucalyptus as a fast-growing plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that eucalyptus grows rapidly.

rubric.why: Tests the plant's role in reducing waterlogging.
rubric.description: Explains that eucalyptus absorbs large amounts of water and can help drain waterlogged land.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking its high water uptake with reducing waterlogging or draining the land.

modelAnswer: Eucalyptus is a fast-growing tree that absorbs large quantities of water.
It is planted in waterlogged areas because it helps drain excess water from the soil.

items.followUp: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and what is exchanged?

rubric.description: States that crossing over is the exchange of segments of genetic material between homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the exchange of chromosome segments or genetic material between homologous chromosomes.

rubric.why: Tests the biological importance of crossing over.
rubric.description: Explains that crossing over produces new gene combinations and increases genetic variation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it creates new gene combinations or increases genetic variation among offspring.

modelAnswer: During prophase I of meiosis, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments of genetic material.
This produces new combinations of genes and increases genetic variation.

items.followUp: What is a bivalent, and during which stage of meiosis is it formed?

rubric.description: Defines synapsis as the pairing of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the pairing or coming together of homologous chromosomes.

rubric.why: Tests where synapsis occurs in meiosis.
rubric.description: Locates synapsis in prophase I, specifically the zygotene stage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating prophase I or, more specifically, zygotene.

modelAnswer: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes.
It occurs during prophase I of meiosis, specifically in the zygotene stage.

items.followUp: How many daughter cells are produced by meiosis, and how does their chromosome number compare with the parent cell?

rubric.why: Tests the definition and outcome of meiosis.
rubric.description: Defines meiosis as a reduction division that produces haploid cells with half the chromosome number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing meiosis as reduction division or stating that it produces four haploid daughter cells with half the parent cell's chromosome number.

rubric.why: Tests recall of the scientist associated with the discovery of meiosis.
rubric.description: Names Oscar Hertwig as the discoverer of meiosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Oscar Hertwig.

modelAnswer: Meiosis is a reduction division in which one diploid cell produces four haploid daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell.
Meiosis was discovered by Oscar Hertwig in 1876.

items.followUp: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.

rubric.why: Tests the electron-transfer definition of oxidation.
rubric.description: States that oxidation is the loss of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining oxidation as loss of electrons.

rubric.why: Tests the paired nature of oxidation and reduction in a redox reaction.
rubric.description: Explains that reduction is gain of electrons and that oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the two processes occur together; accept the electron-transfer definition of reduction when it is correctly paired with oxidation.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, while reduction is the gain of electrons.
In a reaction, oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously; therefore, it is called a redox reaction.
